$comment: The vocabulary this tool uses, defined once and read by both the visualizer (DocsModal) and the CLI (`tt explain`), so the two can never drift apart. Every term here appears somewhere in the UI or command output; if a term is added there, add it here.

concepts.short: One thing your agent setup can do
concepts.long: Every MCP server, agent, skill, provider, model and command in your config becomes a capability. So do the nodes of the curated tech tree. A capability is the unit everything else is measured against.

concepts.short: How far up the tree a capability sits
concepts.long: The tech tree runs through seven eras: Foundation, Model Access, Tool Use, Memory, Autonomy, Assurance, Sovereignty. Later eras depend on earlier ones — you cannot run fully offline before you have a local runtime. Eras describe ordering, not importance.
concepts.seen: Column headers in the ERAS view

concepts.short: Where you are on a tech tree node
concepts.long: Reached: something in your config provides this, and the graph records which capability proved it. Next: prerequisites are met but nothing was detected — this is the useful frontier, and `tt near` lists it. Blocked: you have the tooling but a prerequisite is missing, e.g. retrieval configured with no vector store. Blocked is usually the most informative of the three.
concepts.seen: Solid nodes are reached; outlined nodes are not

concepts.short: Whether a dependency is required or merely helpful
concepts.long: A hard prerequisite must be in place or the dependent capability cannot work — a model cannot run without its provider. A soft prerequisite strengthens something without gating it. Only hard prerequisites block a node from being reached; both are drawn, with soft ones fainter.

concepts.short: A 0-1 estimate of how established a capability is
concepts.long: Seeded from what kind of thing it is and whether it is enabled, then adjusted as your config changes. It is a rough ordering signal, not a measurement — treat a 0.8 as 'more settled than a 0.5', not as a score that means anything on its own.
concepts.seen: The ring around each node, and MATURITY in the detail panel

concepts.long: `tt decay` ranks capabilities by how long since their configuration last changed. It tracks configuration decisions, not how often you invoke something — a server you use daily but never reconfigure will look static, which is intentional. The question it answers is 'what have I stopped tending', not 'what do I use least'.

concepts.short: A capability many others depend on
concepts.long: Ranked by how many capabilities would be affected if it disappeared. High-leverage to invest in, and risky to leave unmaintained. `tt impact <id>` shows exactly what falls over.

The tech tree nodes are combos, and you can define your own in a `combos` block for things specific to your work. A combo is a judgement about what composes into something new, which is why the tool never invents one from your config.
concepts.seen: tt combos, tt near, tt fork

concepts.short: Proven to work, not just configured
concepts.long: Detection proves a name appears in a config file. Verification runs a declared read-only check and records the result, so a capability can be said to work rather than to exist. Reliability is the share of recorded runs that passed, which is why the history is kept: one success is a weaker claim than forty-seven of fifty. Checks execute, so they live in the repository and run only when asked — never on seed.

concepts.short: Whether it may run, not whether it can
concepts.long: Being technically able to perform an action is not permission to perform it. Authority is tracked separately per capability — observe and execute, each autonomous, confirm, or forbidden — so a reached capability can still require approval. This is what lets a larger technical surface stay governable: the limits are explicit rather than implied.

concepts.short: What the system can do, as of a moment
concepts.long: Every seed records the state of every capability, so the graph can answer what was reachable at a past date rather than only now. `tt since` compares two of those observations. Its useful column is the emergent one: capabilities that became reachable although nothing providing them was added, which happens when prerequisites are satisfied by something else entirely. A per-component changelog cannot show those, because no single change explains one.

concepts.short: The area of work a capability belongs to
concepts.long: infra, devops, backend, frontend, ai-ml, quality, security, or meta. Inferred from the capability's name, which means a stack unlike the keyword table's assumptions will land more things in the meta fallback — that table is the first thing to edit.
concepts.seen: Column grouping, and DOMAIN in the detail panel
